domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Software engineering is the scientific discipline, craft, and operational rigor required to develop, verify, and maintain sustainable software systems throughout decades of organizational and technological evolution. It spans test automation economics, continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, defect prevention, refactoring ergonomics, and software supply chain integrity.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Code is written once, but read, modified, debugged, and reviewed hundreds of times across its production lifecycle. Without rigorous engineering practices—automated test pyramids, mutation testing, trunk-based development, and comprehensive static analysis—every codebase rapidly deteriorates under technical debt, until shipping even trivial bug fixes takes weeks of manual regression testing and causes unpredictable production incidents.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: True software engineering is not writing clever code; it is creating automated feedback loops that make building reliable, verifiable, and maintainable systems the path of least resistance.
coreArchitectureRules: Shift-Left Testing Invariant: The cost to discover and fix a software defect increases by 10x at each subsequent development stage: $10 at the IDE/unit level, $100 in CI, $1,000 in staging, and $10,000+ in production.

The Automated Test Pyramid: Maintain a balanced ratio of fast, deterministic unit tests at the base (70%), focused integration/contract tests in the middle (20%), and minimal end-to-end user journey tests at the peak (10%).
The Boy Scout Rule: Always leave the working module cleaner than you found it. Continuous incremental micro-refactoring prevents the compounding accumulation of technical debt.

Trunk-Based Delivery & Small Batch Size: Keep feature branches short-lived (<24 hours) and integrate continuously into trunk with automated CI gates. Large, long-lived branches cause merge conflicts and hide integration regressions.

Deterministic Reproducibility: Build artifacts, automated tests, and deployment environments must be 100% deterministic and reproducible. Eliminate test flakiness, unpinned dependencies, and environmental drift.

failureModes.name: The Inverted Ice-Cream Cone Test Anti-Pattern
failureModes.description: An engineering organization has almost no unit tests, relying instead on 1,500 brittle, slow end-to-end browser tests that take 4 hours to run in CI and fail randomly on timing glitches.
failureModes.mitigation: Restructure into an automated test pyramid: push assertions down to sub-millisecond unit tests and contract tests, retaining only critical end-to-end happy paths.

failureModes.name: Compounding Technical Debt Paralysis
failureModes.description: Under pressure to meet deadlines, engineers copy-paste code and skip tests. Over two years, technical debt compounds until 80% of engineering capacity is consumed by bug fixes and fire-fighting.
failureModes.mitigation: Dedicate 20% of every sprint to tech debt remediation, track technical debt items in Jira with business cost justification, and enforce zero-defect quality bars.

failureModes.name: CI/CD Pipeline Flakiness Blindness
failureModes.description: Tests fail intermittently due to asynchronous race conditions. Engineers become conditioned to hit 'Rerun failed jobs' until it turns green, completely blinding the team to real production regressions.
failureModes.mitigation: Quarantine flaky tests immediately into an isolated non-blocking suite. Mandate that flaky tests must be fixed or deleted within 48 hours.

failureModes.name: Software Supply Chain Compromise
failureModes.description: A third-party npm or PyPI dependency is compromised with malicious credential-stealing code, which runs inside CI build runners and production containers.
failureModes.mitigation: Pin dependencies with cryptographic lockfiles, generate and audit Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), and scan dependencies in CI with automated tools (Trivy/Snyk).

whenToUse: Any software product intended to operate in production for more than a few weeks with real users or financial consequences.
Teams scaling beyond 3 engineers where interpersonal verbal coordination is insufficient to guarantee code quality.
Regulated industries (healthcare, finance, aerospace) requiring rigorous traceability, automated audit trails, and strict verification.
Platforms undergoing continuous integration and deployment where multiple production releases occur daily.
whenNotToUse: Throwaway prototype hackathon code intended exclusively to validate a business idea in 48 hours before being discarded.
One-off data migration scripts that execute once under manual supervision and are never committed to long-term repositories.
Exhaustive 100% code coverage mandates for trivial auto-generated DTOs, getters, and setters that test nothing meaningful.
Over-engineered abstract test frameworks that obscure what business invariant is actually being verified.

tradeOffs.factor: Unit Test Mocking vs Real In-Memory Containers (Testcontainers)
tradeOffs.pro: Mocking with test doubles yields blazingly fast sub-millisecond unit tests with zero infrastructure dependencies.
tradeOffs.con: Mocks encode assumptions that can drift from real behavior; Testcontainers verify true SQL queries and wire protocols at the cost of slower startup time.

tradeOffs.factor: Trunk-Based Development vs GitFlow / Long-Lived Feature Branches
tradeOffs.pro: Trunk-based development prevents merge hell, accelerates feedback loops, and forces modular feature flagging.
tradeOffs.con: Requires disciplined automated CI test gates and feature flag hygiene; incomplete code is merged into the mainline behind flags.

tradeOffs.factor: Mutation Testing vs Raw Code Coverage Metrics
tradeOffs.pro: Mutation testing (Stryker) tests the quality of assertions by injecting deliberate faults, proving tests actually catch bugs.
tradeOffs.con: Running mutation tests across large codebases is computationally expensive and takes significant CI CPU time.

productionScenarios.title: Eliminating Flaky CI Outages at Scale
productionScenarios.scenario: A 200-engineer engineering department experienced 35% CI failure rates on main branch commits, delaying releases by an average of 4.5 days per sprint.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented automated flaky test quarantine, replaced arbitrary sleep() calls with condition polling, and established a 10-minute CI SLA. PR merge velocity increased by 280% with zero escaped regressions.

productionScenarios.title: Shift-Left Security and Quality Gate Migration
productionScenarios.scenario: A SaaS company discovered critical security CVEs and database migration bugs during production staging deploys right before quarterly customer audits.
productionScenarios.outcome: Shifted checks left into local git pre-commit hooks and PR automation: automated static analysis (ESLint/Sonar), secret scanning, and automated ephemeral database migration dry-runs caught 98% of issues before code review.

coreChallenges.title: The Shift-Left Test Pyramid Economics
coreChallenges.explanation: Finding a defect in production costs 100x more than catching it in unit tests. The automated test pyramid prioritizes fast, deterministic unit and contract tests over slow, flaky end-to-end suites.

coreChallenges.title: End-to-End Test Flakiness & Reliability
coreChallenges.explanation: Flaky tests destroy developer confidence in CI pipelines. Eliminating non-deterministic network calls, asynchronous sleep timers, and shared test state is essential for continuous delivery.

coreChallenges.title: Compounding Technical Debt & Refactoring
coreChallenges.explanation: Technical debt acts like financial debt: short-term shortcuts incur long-term interest that slows feature velocity to a crawl. Regular Boy Scout refactoring keeps codebases agile.

coreChallenges.title: Software Supply Chain & Versioning Rigor
coreChallenges.explanation: Modern applications rely on thousands of third-party dependencies. Semantic versioning, Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), and automated dependency scanning prevent supply chain vulnerabilities.

domainContent.title: Software Engineering

spark.summary: Software engineering is the discipline of designing, verifying, and evolving maintainable software systems through clean modular code, fast deterministic test pyramids, test-driven design, trunk-based CI/CD pipelines, safe legacy refactoring, disciplined code reviews, and automated static analysis.
spark.keyTakeaway: Great software engineering builds automated feedback loops—from IDE linters and sub-millisecond unit tests to hermetic CI/CD pipelines—so shipping reliable, readable changes is the path of least resistance.

domain.purpose: Learn to build and evolve codebases that remain readable, testable, and safe to deploy rapidly as team size, product scope, and system age grow.
audience: Software engineers improving code quality, testability, and delivery speed.
Backend and full-stack engineers rescuing legacy systems or eliminating flaky CI.
Tech leads and staff engineers establishing CI/CD quality gates and engineering standards.
learningOutcomes: Write intention-revealing, side-effect-isolated code using Command-Query Separation and cohesion heuristics.
Balance unit, integration, contract, and end-to-end tests into a fast, deterministic test pyramid.
Use Red-Green-Refactor TDD and the Transformation Priority Premise to drive clean interface design.
Operate trunk-based development with hermetic builds and immutable artifact promotion.
Safely refactor untested legacy code using characterization tests, dependency seams, and Branch by Abstraction.
Run high-signal, small-batch code reviews focused on correctness, invariants, and maintainability.
Enforce automated quality gates with SAST, cyclomatic/cognitive complexity budgets, and mutation testing.

learningJourney.title: Engineering Craftsmanship & Clean Code
learningJourney.purpose: Write code optimized for human comprehension by isolating side effects, preserving clear abstractions, and applying DRY, KISS, YAGNI, and the Boy Scout Rule.
learningJourney.explanation: Code is written once but read, debugged, and modified dozens of times. Clean code is not about clever one-liners or premature patterns; it is about reducing cognitive load. Intention-revealing names encode domain units and invariants, Command-Query Separation (CQS) ensures functions either mutate state or return data without hidden side effects, and pure core functions keep I/O at the edges. Apply DRY to business knowledge rather than incidental code duplication—two functions that look similar today but evolve for different business reasons should remain separate.

ideas.title: Command-Query Separation & Pure Cores
ideas.description: Separate deterministic domain calculations from side-effecting I/O (DB writes, HTTP calls, clock reads). Pure functions require zero mocks to test and cannot corrupt shared state.

ideas.title: Knowledge DRY vs Incidental Duplication
ideas.description: Avoid coupling unrelated domains through a shared helper just because two snippets look alike today; wrong abstractions are far more expensive than three lines of duplicated code.

example.title: Untangling a 400-Line Billing Method with Pure Domain Extraction
example.scenario: A monthly invoicing function mixed tax calculation, discount eligibility, SQL updates, and email sending in a single nested loop, causing frequent off-by-one rounding bugs that required a live database to reproduce.
example.reasoning: The team extracted pure functions for prorated line-item calculation and tax rules (returning immutable value objects) while keeping database persistence and email dispatch in a thin orchestrator. Unit tests for edge cases like leap years and negative credits dropped from 4 seconds to 2 milliseconds.
example.lesson: Separating pure business rules from I/O side effects makes correctness obvious to readers and trivial to verify.

caveats: Never apply the Boy Scout Rule so aggressively inside a bugfix PR that unrelated formatting diffs obscure the actual behavioral change.
YAGNI applies to speculative extensibility, not to basic input validation, logging, or error handling.
reflectionQuestions: Which functions in your hot path both mutate state and return calculated results?
Can you test your core business logic without booting a database, HTTP server, or clock mock?
Where has premature DRY coupled two features that actually change for different reasons?
Does a new engineer reading this module understand its invariants without tracing five other files?

learningJourney.title: The Automated Testing Pyramid
learningJourney.purpose: Structure verification into fast, deterministic unit tests, realistic Testcontainers/contract tests, and minimal end-to-end journeys.
learningJourney.explanation: Defect remediation cost grows exponentially the later a bug is caught—from seconds in an IDE to costly production rollbacks. The Automated Testing Pyramid optimizes feedback speed and signal-to-noise: a broad base (~70%) of sub-millisecond, isolated unit tests; a focused middle (~20%) of integration tests (using ephemeral Testcontainers for real SQL/Redis behavior) and consumer-driven contract tests (Pact/OpenAPI); and a thin peak (~10%) of critical end-to-end user journeys. Inverting this into an 'Ice-Cream Cone' of hundreds of brittle browser tests creates multi-hour CI queues and chronic flakiness.

benefits: Execute in milliseconds with zero network or disk I/O.
Pinpoint exact logic regressions and edge cases immediately.
costs: Do not verify SQL queries, serialization formats, or third-party wire protocols.

benefits: Testcontainers verify real database migrations, indexes, and queries.
Contract tests catch breaking API schema changes without booting full environments.
costs: Slower container startup (seconds) and higher CI memory footprint.

benefits: Verify full-stack wiring across UI, auth, APIs, and persistence.
costs: Slowest execution and highest susceptibility to timing and environment flakiness.

ideas.title: Determinism Invariant
ideas.description: Eliminate Thread.sleep()/setTimeout() polling guesses, shared mutable fixtures, and real wall-clock dependencies; inject deterministic clocks and use explicit condition-polling assertions.

ideas.title: Consumer-Driven Contract Testing
ideas.description: Verify producer-consumer API compatibility in CI via Pact or schema registries rather than maintaining fragile staging environments where all microservices must be deployed simultaneously.

example.title: Reversing a 90-Minute Flaky E2E Suite into a 7-Minute Pyramid
example.scenario: A 60-engineer SaaS org relied on 1,200 Selenium end-to-end tests that took 90 minutes in CI and failed 30% of the time on network timeouts, prompting engineers to blindly click 'Rerun'.
example.reasoning: The team moved validation, pricing, and permission assertions down into unit tests, replaced cross-service E2E checks with Pact contract tests and PostgreSQL Testcontainers, and kept only 25 critical-path E2E smoke tests. CI runtime dropped to 7 minutes with <1% flakiness.
example.lesson: Push every assertion as far down the test pyramid as possible while still verifying the real boundary behavior.

reflectionQuestions: What percentage of your CI failures are caused by flaky tests rather than real regressions?
Which E2E tests are actually verifying pure business logic that belongs in unit tests?
Are database queries and migrations tested against a real engine (Testcontainers) or an in-memory mock that diverges in SQL dialect?
How do you catch breaking API contract changes before deploying two services to staging?

learningJourney.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) Mastery
learningJourney.purpose: Use the Red-Green-Refactor loop and Transformation Priority Premise to drive modular, loosely coupled API design before writing implementation.
learningJourney.explanation: Test-Driven Development is primarily a design discipline rather than a coverage metric. In the Red phase, writing a failing test forces you to specify the caller's ergonomics, inputs, and edge-case contracts before committing to internal data structures. In the Green phase, you write the simplest code to pass—guided by the Transformation Priority Premise (TPP), moving from constants to variables to conditionals to recursion—avoiding premature generality. In the Refactor phase, with a green safety net, you eliminate duplication and sharpen abstractions. Over-mocking internal collaborators (London/mockist style) couples tests to implementation details; testing through public module boundaries (Detroit/classicist style) keeps refactoring painless.

architectureFlow.name: 1. Red (Specify Behavior)
architectureFlow.description: Write a small, failing test describing one concrete requirement or edge case at the module boundary.

architectureFlow.name: 2. Green (Minimal Implementation)
architectureFlow.description: Write the simplest code needed to pass the test without speculative abstractions.

architectureFlow.name: 3. Refactor (Clean Structure)
architectureFlow.description: Improve naming, extract pure helpers, and remove duplication while keeping all tests green.

architectureFlow.name: 4. Repeat in Small Increments
architectureFlow.description: Advance step-by-step using TPP rather than designing a rigid monolith upfront.

ideas.title: Test Behavior, Not Implementation
ideas.description: Assert observable outputs and state transitions at the public boundary; avoid mocking private helpers or verifying internal call counts that break on every refactor.

ideas.title: Transformation Priority Premise (TPP)
ideas.description: Prefer simpler code transformations (null -> constant -> scalar -> conditional -> iteration) as you make each new test pass so algorithms emerge cleanly without getting stuck.

example.title: Designing a Rate-Limiter Token Bucket via Red-Green-Refactor
example.scenario: An engineer needed to build an in-memory token bucket rate limiter with burst capacity, continuous refill, and clock-skew safety.
example.reasoning: Starting with a test for an empty bucket, then a single refill tick, then fractional elapsed seconds, and finally burst capping forced a clean Clock interface injection from test #1. The resulting 50-line class had zero hidden time.now() calls and 100% deterministic edge-case coverage.
example.lesson: Writing the test first immediately exposes hidden dependencies like system clocks, randomness, and global state.

reflectionQuestions: When a function is hard to write a unit test for, is the problem the test framework or the function's hidden dependencies?
Do your tests break when you rename private methods or change internal data structures without changing behavior?
Are you writing tests after the fact that merely mirror implementation bugs, or specifying invariants first?
Which external boundaries (clocks, random generators, gateways) should be injected to keep TDD loops fast?

supportingConcepts.title: TDD as a Design Tool, Not a Testing Tool

learningJourney.title: Continuous Integration & Delivery (CI/CD)
learningJourney.purpose: Ship small, reversible increments safely using trunk-based development, hermetic builds, immutable artifact promotion, and automated deployment gates.
learningJourney.explanation: Continuous Integration means merging small, verified changes into the main trunk at least daily, eliminating the integration hell of long-lived GitFlow branches. Incomplete features are decoupled from deployment via runtime feature flags and expand-and-contract database migrations (add nullable column -> dual-write -> backfill -> switch reads -> drop old column). Builds must be hermetic and reproducible—pinning dependencies via cryptographic lockfiles and generating a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)—and the exact immutable container digest built in CI is promoted unchanged from staging to canary to production.

benefits: Small, frequent merges eliminate multi-week merge conflicts.
Forces modular decoupling via feature flags and backward-compatible migrations.
costs: Requires fast, reliable CI gates and strict discipline to clean up stale feature flags.

benefits: Isolates unfinished work from main without runtime feature flags.
costs: Causes painful merge conflicts, delayed integration bugs, and large risky release batches.

ideas.title: Build Once, Promote Everywhere
ideas.description: Never rebuild source code per environment; compile and sign a single immutable container image digest (sha256) and inject environment-specific config at runtime.

ideas.title: Zero-Downtime Expand-and-Contract Migrations
ideas.description: Separate schema expansion from old-column removal across deployments so rolling upgrades and instant rollbacks never fail on missing columns.

example.title: Eliminating Release Freezes with Trunk-Based Delivery & Canary Rollouts
example.scenario: A fintech team used 3-week release branches in GitFlow; every bi-weekly release required a 2-day code freeze and manual QA sign-off, yet still caused 4-hour rollback incidents.
example.reasoning: The team adopted trunk-based development with <24-hour PRs, automated ephemeral preview environments, expand-and-contract DB migrations, and Argo Rollouts canary analysis (auto-aborting if error rate >0.5% or p99 >250ms). Deployment frequency rose from bi-weekly to 15 times daily.
example.lesson: Small batch sizes plus automated canary rollback reduce both deployment risk and mean time to recovery.

reflectionQuestions: How many days does an average branch live before merging to main, and how often do merge conflicts occur?
Are staging and production running the exact same immutable artifact digest built in CI?
Can you roll back a code deployment in under 2 minutes without breaking database schema compatibility?
Are third-party build dependencies pinned by cryptographic hash and scanned for supply-chain CVEs?

learningJourney.title: Refactoring & Legacy Code Rescue
learningJourney.purpose: Modify untested legacy systems safely using characterization tests, dependency seams, and incremental Branch by Abstraction.
learningJourney.explanation: Michael Feathers defines legacy code simply as code without tests. Editing it directly creates the Legacy Code Dilemma: you need tests to refactor safely, but you often must refactor to introduce tests. Break this deadlock by first writing characterization (golden master) tests that record the system's actual current behavior—quirks included—before changing logic. Next, identify seams (link, object, or parameter seams) to break hardcoded static calls or database dependencies without altering behavior. For large structural replacements, use Branch by Abstraction: introduce an interface over the legacy module, route a new implementation behind a feature flag, shadow-compare outputs, and delete the legacy path only after parity is proven.

ideas.title: Characterization (Golden Master) Tests
ideas.description: Capture representative production inputs and assert the exact outputs of the legacy module today so accidental behavioral shifts are caught immediately during cleanup.

ideas.title: Branch by Abstraction
ideas.description: Wrap a tangled legacy subsystem behind a clean abstraction, build the replacement incrementally behind a toggle, validate parity in production, and retire the old code without a risky big-bang rewrite.

example.title: Replacing a Legacy Pricing Engine Without Downtime
example.scenario: An e-commerce platform's 10-year-old discount engine had zero unit tests and subtle rounding quirks that downstream accounting reports depended on.
example.reasoning: Engineers recorded 5,000 real cart snapshots as characterization tests, wrapped the engine behind a PricingPort seam, and used Branch by Abstraction to shadow-run the new engine against live traffic. Discrepancies were fixed before cutting over 100% of traffic.
example.lesson: Never rewrite legacy code in the dark; pin its current behavior with characterization tests and migrate behind an abstraction seam.

caveats: Resist 'big-bang rewrites'—they freeze feature delivery while inevitably re-introducing forgotten edge-case fixes.
Keep structural refactoring commits separate from behavioral feature commits so git bisect and code review remain clear.
reflectionQuestions: Which high-churn legacy module currently has zero automated tests protecting its behavior?
What minimal seam (parameter injection, wrapper interface, or extract-and-override) lets you test this module in isolation?
How will you verify that a refactored replacement preserves undocumented edge-case behavior?
Can you migrate traffic incrementally via Branch by Abstraction instead of a single cutover PR?

supportingConcepts.title: Michael Feathers' Definition of Legacy Code

learningJourney.title: Code Review Rigor & Team Collaboration
learningJourney.purpose: Maximize defect detection and shared ownership through small pull requests, automated style checks, and high-signal reviewer checklists.
learningJourney.explanation: Code review exists to catch logic flaws, security gaps, and architectural drift while spreading system knowledge across the team. Review effectiveness collapses when pull requests exceed ~300-400 lines: reviewers skim and default to 'LGTM'. High-performing teams automate formatting, imports, and lint rules in pre-commit/CI so human reviewers never waste cycles on whitespace. Reviewers follow a structured checklist—verifying correctness, edge cases, failure handling, security boundaries, and test quality—and distinguish blocking defects from optional nitpicks.

ideas.title: Small-Batch PR Ergonomics (<300 LOC)
ideas.description: Decompose large features into stacked or sequential small PRs (schema migration, core logic, API wiring) so each review takes 10 minutes and receives deep scrutiny.

ideas.title: Automate Formatting, Humanize Design Review
ideas.description: Offload style and syntax rules to Prettier/Black/Spotless in CI; focus human review on concurrency safety, data invariants, error paths, and operational observability.

example.title: Cutting PR Turnaround Time by 65% via Stacked Small PRs
example.scenario: A backend team averaged 4 days per PR review because engineers routinely opened 1,500-line feature PRs mixing migrations, refactoring, and business logic.
example.reasoning: The team instituted a 350-line soft cap, automated formatting/linting in pre-commit, added a PR template requiring test evidence and rollback notes, and labeled minor comments as 'nit:'. Median time-to-first-review dropped from 26 hours to 3 hours.
example.lesson: Small, focused pull requests with automated style checks turn code review from a bottleneck into a fast quality multiplier.

reflectionQuestions: What is the median line count and wait time of pull requests on your team?
How many review comments in the last month were about formatting or naming rules that a linter could enforce?
Do reviewers explicitly check concurrency, idempotency, and failure-path test coverage?
Are blocking architectural concerns clearly separated from non-blocking suggestions?

learningJourney.title: Static Analysis, Linters & Mutation Testing
learningJourney.purpose: Catch security flaws, complexity creep, and weak test assertions automatically using AST-based SAST, complexity budgets, and mutation testing.
learningJourney.explanation: Line coverage only proves that a test executed a line—not that it asserted anything meaningful about the result. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools like Semgrep, CodeQL, and SonarQube parse Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) and data-flow graphs to detect SQL injection, tainted inputs, null dereferences, and excessive cyclomatic or cognitive complexity before code review. Mutation testing (PIT for Java, Stryker for JS/TS, mutmut for Python) goes a step further: it systematically injects small faults (flipping > to >=, removing return values, negating conditionals) and measures the mutation score—the percentage of mutants killed by failing tests.

ideas.title: Cognitive Complexity Budgets
ideas.description: Track cognitive complexity (nested conditionals, early-return violations) rather than raw line count so deeply tangled methods are flagged automatically in CI.

ideas.title: Mutation Score Over Raw Line Coverage
ideas.description: Run mutation testing on critical domain and financial modules to expose tests that execute code without asserting boundary conditions.

example.title: Exposing Hollow Tests in a Billing Engine with PIT Mutation Testing
example.scenario: A Java billing service boasted 92% JaCoCo line coverage, yet a subtle off-by-one bug in tiered pricing overcharged enterprise customers in production.
example.reasoning: Running PIT mutation testing on the pricing package revealed a 48% mutation score—existing tests executed the tier-boundary branches without asserting exact boundary values. Adding targeted boundary assertions raised the mutation score to 91% and caught two latent rounding bugs.
example.lesson: Line coverage measures execution; mutation testing measures whether your assertions actually detect bugs.

caveats: Run mutation testing incrementally on changed files or critical packages in CI rather than across an entire monorepo on every commit.
Treat SAST rules as curated team invariants; disable noisy false-positive rules so engineers do not ignore real security alerts.
reflectionQuestions: Which critical modules have high line coverage but have never been checked for assertion strength?
What SAST and secret-scanning checks run locally or in CI before a human ever opens a PR?
Where is cyclomatic or cognitive complexity highest in your codebase, and does it correlate with bug frequency?
How do you prevent new architectural boundary violations or tainted-input vulnerabilities from entering main?

endToEndExample.title: Modernize a High-Defect Monorepo Delivery Pipeline
endToEndExample.scenario: A 120-engineer product organization suffers 30% flaky CI failures, 3-week release cycles on long-lived branches, and recurring regressions in an untested legacy billing module.

architectureFlow.name: Local IDE & Pre-Commit Gate
architectureFlow.responsibility: Runs formatting, AST SAST rules, and secret scanning in seconds before code is pushed.

architectureFlow.name: Fast PR Verification (<10 min)
architectureFlow.responsibility: Executes isolated unit tests, Testcontainers DB migrations, contract tests, and incremental mutation checks.

architectureFlow.name: Hermetic Trunk Build & SBOM
architectureFlow.responsibility: Produces a single signed immutable container image digest and dependency lockfile audit on merge to main.

architectureFlow.name: Canary & Feature-Flagged Rollout
architectureFlow.responsibility: Promotes the immutable artifact through staging to 5% canary with automated error-budget rollback.

reasoning: Quarantine flaky E2E tests immediately and replace sleep() calls with deterministic polling and Testcontainers.
Wrap the legacy billing module in characterization tests and extract pure calculation functions behind a seam.
Enforce <350-line PRs on trunk-based development, decoupling incomplete work with feature flags.
Introduce expand-and-contract database migrations so code rollbacks never break schema compatibility.
Run Semgrep SAST and dependency CVE scanning in CI, plus PIT/Stryker mutation testing on critical financial packages.
Promote the exact same signed container digest across environments and gate production rollout on canary SLOs.
lessons: Speed and reliability reinforce each other: fast, deterministic CI enables small batches, which reduce defect rates.
Quarantining flaky tests restores trust in red builds so engineers never normalize clicking 'Rerun'.
Characterization tests and seams let teams modernize legacy cores incrementally without risky rewrites.
Automated formatting and SAST free human code reviewers to focus on invariants, concurrency, and domain clarity.
Mutation testing on high-risk modules catches hollow assertions that 90% line coverage hides.

failureScenario.title: Non-Backward-Compatible Migration Blocks Emergency Rollback
failureScenario.reasoning: A PR renames a database column and updates application code in the same release. When a latency regression forces an immediate rollback to the previous container image, the old code crashes because the original column was already dropped.
failureScenario.recovery: Enforce expand-and-contract migrations in CI: add the new column and dual-write in Release 1, backfill and switch reads in Release 2, and drop the legacy column only in Release 3 after the rollback window closes.

decisionFramework.question: Is business logic separated from I/O and framework side effects?
decisionFramework.reason: Pure domain functions can be tested in milliseconds without brittle mocks or live databases.

decisionFramework.question: Does this check belong at the unit, integration, contract, or E2E layer?
decisionFramework.reason: Push verification as far down the test pyramid as possible to keep CI under 10 minutes and eliminate flakiness.

decisionFramework.question: Can this change be merged to trunk behind a flag or compatible schema?
decisionFramework.reason: Small daily merges and expand-and-contract migrations prevent merge debt and enable instant rollbacks.

decisionFramework.question: Are existing behaviors pinned before refactoring legacy code?
decisionFramework.reason: Characterization tests and seams protect undocumented production invariants during structural cleanup.

decisionFramework.question: Can an automated gate enforce this rule instead of a human reviewer?
decisionFramework.reason: Use linters, SAST, lockfiles, and mutation testing for mechanical rules so reviewers focus on design and correctness.

knowledgeCheck.question: A payment service has 90% line coverage from unit tests that heavily mock internal helper methods, yet production releases frequently break on SQL syntax errors and subtle rounding bugs. What is the best diagnosis?

options.text: Mocks hide real database behavior and line coverage does not prove assertion quality; add Testcontainers integration tests and mutation testing on pricing logic.
options.feedback: Correct. Mocking persistence hides real SQL/migration issues, and high line coverage without strong boundary assertions leaves rounding bugs undetected.

options.text: Increase the unit test line coverage mandate from 90% to 100% across all DTOs and mocks.
options.feedback: Chasing 100% line coverage with mocks will not catch SQL dialect bugs or weak assertions.

options.text: Replace all unit tests with 500 end-to-end browser tests so every request hits the real database.
options.feedback: Inverting the pyramid into hundreds of slow E2E tests creates multi-hour flaky CI pipelines.

exercises.title: Rescue an Untested Legacy Module
exercises.prompt: Outline a step-by-step plan to add characterization tests, introduce a dependency seam, and extract pure domain logic from a 500-line untested service class.
reviewQuestions: How do you capture current edge-case behavior before editing logic?
Which seam breaks the hardcoded database or HTTP dependency?
How do you keep refactoring PRs small and reviewable?

exercises.title: Fix an Inverted Test Pyramid
exercises.prompt: A team has 800 flaky E2E tests taking 75 minutes and 50 unit tests. Redesign the verification strategy using unit tests, Testcontainers, and contract tests.
reviewQuestions: Which assertions move down to sub-millisecond unit tests?
How do you verify cross-service API compatibility without a shared staging environment?
What policy handles a newly detected flaky test?

exercises.title: Design a Trunk-Based Expand-and-Contract Rollout
exercises.prompt: Plan a zero-downtime column split and API v2 rollout using trunk-based development, feature flags, and immutable artifact promotion.
reviewQuestions: How many deployments are required to safely rename or split a column?
What guarantees that staging and production run the exact same binary?
What canary metrics trigger an automated rollback?

domainContent.finalSummary: Sustainable software engineering relies on fast, automated feedback loops: clean pure cores, a deterministic test pyramid, TDD-driven interfaces, trunk-based hermetic CI/CD, safe legacy seams, small code reviews, and static/mutation quality gates.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Software engineering is the discipline of designing, verifying, and evolving maintainable software systems through clean modular code, fast deterministic test pyramids, test-driven design, trunk-based CI/CD pipelines, safe legacy refactoring, disciplined code reviews, and automated static analysis.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Hermetic Trunk Build & SBOM applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Canary & Feature-Flagged Rol.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: **Non-Backward-Compatible Migration Blocks Emergency Rollback** — A PR renames a database column and updates application code in the same release. When a latency regression forces an immediate rollback to the previous container image, the old code crashes because the original column was already dropped. **Recovery:** Enforce expand-and-contract migrations in CI: add the new column and dual-write in Release 1, backfill and switch reads in Release 2, and drop the legacy column only in Release 3 after the rollback window closes.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Great software engineering builds automated feedback loops—from IDE linters and sub-millisecond unit tests to hermetic CI/CD pipelines—so shipping reliable, readable changes is the path of least resistance.

tipsAndTricks: Domain principle: Great software engineering builds automated feedback loops—from IDE linters and sub-millisecond unit tests to hermetic CI/CD pipelines—so shipping reliable, readable changes is the path of least resistance.
End-to-end lesson: Speed and reliability reinforce each other: fast, deterministic CI enables small batches, which reduce defect rates.
